prompt: Which reduced fractions terminate in binary? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. Its denominator is a power of two.
The denominator contains a factor of five, so the binary digits repeat.
Correct. Eight is a power of two; the fraction terminates.
Five is not a power of two, so the expansion repeats.
Correct. Repeated halving reaches this fraction exactly.

workedExample: Inspect the denominators after reduction. Powers of two match binary fraction positions; a factor of five cannot be removed by adding finitely many such positions. A particular storage format must still have enough precision and range.

prompt: A binary conversion of decimal one tenth returns to a nonzero fractional remainder it encountered earlier. What follows?

options.text: The same sequence of digits will repeat
options.explanation: Correct. Each step starts from the same remainder and applies the same rule, so it repeats the same next digits.

options.text: One more binary digit must make the value exact
options.explanation: A repeated nonzero remainder does not approach a terminating step.

options.text: The processor has made an arithmetic error
options.explanation: An exact conversion can repeat because the fraction has no finite binary expansion.

options.text: Using hexadecimal instead will make the finite stored bits exact
options.explanation: Changing the display does not add bits or remove the repeating binary tail.

workedExample: The conversion state is its remaining fraction. Repeating that state repeats the later steps. More finite bits can improve an approximation, but cannot store one tenth exactly as a finite binary fraction.
